title: Can a sealed class permit a subclass in a different package (module vs non-module rules)?
shortTitle: Can a sealed class permit a subclass in a different package (module vs non-module rules)?

s1_definition.profdef: It depends on whether the code is in a named module. If the sealed type and its permitted subtypes belong to the same named module, the permitted subtypes may be declared in different packages of that module. If the code is on the unnamed-module classpath, all permitted subtypes must be in the same package as the sealed type. In every case the permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type — a sealed hierarchy can never span two different modules.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's head office declares the closed list of account products. If the whole bank operates as one unified organisation (a module), head office may place the approved products in different departments (packages) across that organisation, as long as they all belong to the bank. But if the bank is just a loose collection of branches with no central organisation (the classpath), head office can only approve products kept in the very same department (same package) as the master policy document. And no matter what, an approved product can never belong to a completely different bank (a different module).
s1_definition.oneliner: Same module, different packages is allowed; classpath requires the same package; different modules is never allowed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** It depends on whether the code is in a named module. If the sealed type and its permitted subtypes belong to the same named module, the permitted subtypes may be declared in different packages of that module. If the code is on the unnamed-module classpath, all permitted subtypes must be in the same package as the sealed type. In every case the permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type — a sealed hierarchy can never span two different modules.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's head office declares the closed list of account products. If the whole bank operates as one unified organisation (a module), head office may place the approved products in different departments (packages) across that organisation, as long as they all belong to the bank. But if the bank is just a loose collection of branches with no central organisation (the classpath), head office can only approve products kept in the very same department (same package) as the master policy document. And no matter what, an approved product can never belong to a completely different bank (a different module).

**One line to remember:** Same module, different packages is allowed; classpath requires the same package; different modules is never allowed.

sections.s2_technical:
The sealed-class rule for subtype location was designed to balance encapsulation with practicality. The fixed, universal part is that **all permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type**. A sealed hierarchy is a closed, author-controlled design, and allowing it to cross module boundaries would let another module insert itself into your closed family, defeating the purpose. So the compiler never lets a permitted subtype live in a different module.

Within a **named module**, the rule relaxes on packages: permitted subtypes may be in **different packages of the same module**. This is because a module is itself a strong encapsulation boundary, so the author already controls everything inside the module. For example, a module `com.bank.accounts` can declare `sealed interface Account` in package `com.bank.accounts.api` and permit `LoanAccount` in package `com.bank.accounts.loan`, as long as both packages are in the same module. This lets you organise a sealed hierarchy across a clean package structure.

On the **classpath**, meaning the unnamed module, the rule is stricter: all permitted subtypes must be in the **same package** as the sealed type. Without a module boundary, the package is the only encapsulation unit the compiler can rely on, so it requires the whole sealed family to sit in one package. If you try to permit a subtype from another package on the classpath, you get a compile error such as "class is in a different package from its sealed supertype."

The practical consequence is that **modularising** your application unlocks cleaner package organisation for sealed hierarchies. A library author shipping a modular JAR can spread a sealed type and its subtypes across several packages for readability, exporting only the API package while keeping subtypes in internal packages. A non-modular application forced onto the classpath must keep the whole family in one package, which can feel cramped for large hierarchies.

A senior nuance is that the permitted subtypes must also be **accessible** to the sealed type at compile time, which interacts with module exports: even within a module the subtypes are visible because module-internal access does not require exporting, but across the module's public API you export only what callers need. Another nuance is that this rule is checked by the compiler and also recorded in the `PermittedSubclasses` class-file attribute, and the JVM re-validates at load time, so you cannot smuggle in a cross-module subtype through bytecode. A final nuance is that this is one more reason real production banking systems adopt JPMS modules: it gives sealed hierarchies both strong encapsulation and flexible package layout, which matters when modelling large closed domains like transaction types or regulatory states.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants to model account products as a sealed hierarchy, but for clean architecture it wants the sealed `Account` interface in an `api` package and the concrete products in a `products` package. The bank needs to know whether this cross-package layout is allowed. It is allowed only if everything lives in the same named module. This shows the module rule.

Problem 2 — The bank's older code runs on the plain classpath without modules. There, the same cross-package attempt fails to compile, forcing all subtypes into one package. We show why and the error that results.

Problem 3 — A third-party vendor module tries to add its own permitted subtype to the bank's sealed `Account`. This is impossible because a sealed hierarchy cannot cross modules, protecting the bank's closed product set from outside tampering. We illustrate the boundary.

In the mini-project we present a modular layout where the sealed `Account` is in one package and its permitted subtypes are in another package of the same module, a `module-info.java` describing the module, and a demo that uses the accounts. We explain in comments the classpath restriction and the cross-module prohibition.

The code contains: a module descriptor, a sealed `Account` in an `api` package, permitted subtypes in a `products` package, and a runnable demo.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile as a MODULE (Java 17+). Cross-package permits is allowed here.
javac -d target/classes $(find src/main/java -name '*.java')

# Run as a module
java --module-path target/classes -m com.bank.accounts/com.bank.accounts.CrossPackageDemo

# If compiled on the plain CLASSPATH with subtypes in a different package,
# javac would FAIL with: "class ... is in a different package from its sealed supertype"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three accounts — savings for Rajesh, current for Priya, loan for Rajesh — defined across two packages within one module.

Step 1 — The module `com.bank.accounts` is compiled. The sealed `Account` interface lives in the `api` package and permits three subtypes that live in the `products` package. Because both packages belong to the same named module, the compiler accepts the cross-package permits.

Step 2 — `main` creates one instance of each permitted subtype. Each object is a valid `Account`, and the type system knows the complete, closed set even though the subtypes sit in a different package from the interface.

Step 3 — The loop logs each account's simple class name, id, holder, and balance. All three print normally, demonstrating that the cross-package modular layout works at runtime.

Step 4 — Comments then explain the two boundaries. On the plain classpath, the same layout would fail to compile because subtypes would have to share the `api` package. And a subtype from a different module could never be permitted, so an outside vendor cannot inject a new account product into the bank's sealed hierarchy.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  MODULE com.bank.accounts
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  package api                                                │
  │    sealed interface Account permits                         │
  │       SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, LoanAccount           │
  │                     │ cross-package permit (SAME MODULE ✓)  │
  │  package products   ▼                                       │
  │    final SavingsAccount  final CurrentAccount  final LoanAccount │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CLASSPATH (no module):
    Account in api  +  subtype in products  → ❌ compile error
    all permitted subtypes MUST be in package api (same package)

  DIFFERENT MODULE:
    vendor module subtype → ❌ never permitted (hierarchy cannot span modules)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Permitted Subtype Location Rules ═══

  ┌─ Rules ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ALWAYS: permitted subtypes in SAME MODULE as sealed type      │
  │ named module: subtypes may be in DIFFERENT packages           │
  │ classpath (unnamed module): subtypes in SAME package          │
  │ never: subtype in a DIFFERENT module                          │
  │ recorded in PermittedSubclasses attr; JVM re-validates        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  module com.bank.accounts
  ┌──────────────────────────┐   permits (cross-package OK)
  │ api.Account (sealed)      │──────────────┐
  │ + id/holder/balance       │              │
  └──────────────────────────┘              ▼
                               ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                               │ products.SavingsAccount(final)│
                               │ products.CurrentAccount(final)│
                               │ products.LoanAccount(final)   │
                               └──────────────────────────────┘

  Call Chain:
    1. compile module → cross-package permits accepted
    2. new SavingsAccount(...) is-a Account
    3. loop logs each account
    4. classpath variant → compile error (different package)
    5. cross-module subtype → rejected
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The answer is: it depends on modules. The one universal rule is that all permitted subtypes of a sealed type must live in the same module as the sealed type. A sealed hierarchy is a closed, author-controlled family, and letting it cross module boundaries would allow another module to insert itself into my closed set, which defeats the whole point, so the compiler never permits a subtype from a different module.

Within a single named module the rule relaxes on packages, so permitted subtypes may be declared in different packages of that same module. The reason is that the module is itself a strong encapsulation boundary, so I already control everything inside it. In my banking project I put the sealed Account interface in an api package and the concrete products in a products package, and because both packages are in the same account module, the cross-package permits compiles cleanly. I then export only the api package and keep the products package internal, which is nice for architecture.

On the plain classpath, meaning the unnamed module, the rule is stricter: all permitted subtypes must be in the same package as the sealed type. Without a module boundary the package is the only encapsulation unit the compiler can trust, so the whole family must sit in one package, and trying to permit a subtype from another package gives a compile error saying the class is in a different package from its sealed supertype.

The practical lesson I give is that modularising unlocks a cleaner package layout for sealed hierarchies while still keeping them strongly closed, which is exactly what a bank wants for a large closed domain such as account products or transaction states. The module boundary also means an outside vendor module can never inject a new permitted account type into our sealed Account, so our product set stays protected. And because the permitted set is recorded in the class file and re-validated by the JVM at load time, nobody can smuggle in a cross-module subtype through bytecode either.
